title: 〜は〜です — "X is Y"
explanation: X は Y です means "X is Y". は marks the topic, the thing you are talking about, and here it is said "wa", not "ha"; です at the end is the polite "is / am / are" and never changes for I, you or they. When the topic is obvious, leave it out: がくせいです alone means "I'm a student." Put さん after other people's names but never after your own, and call your own wife and husband つま and おっと, but someone else's おくさん and ごしゅじん. Two look-alikes come later: も replaces は to mean "too", and が also marks a subject but puts the spotlight on it.

title: 〜ですか — asking questions
explanation: Put か at the end of a です sentence and it becomes a question; the word order stays the same, and か does the job of the question mark. Answer with はい or いいえ, or with そうです ("that's right") and ちがいます ("no, that's not right"). To ask "what" or "who", put なん / なに or だれ exactly where the answer will go: しごとは なんですか → しごとは せんせいです. This is the polite way to ask; between partners a rising voice without か comes later with casual speech. Don't mix it up with か between two nouns, which means "or".

title: 〜の〜 — "X's Y"
explanation: の links two nouns, and the first one describes the second: わたしの かさ is "my umbrella", おっとの かばん is "my husband's bag". It also tells where something is from or what kind it is: にほんの くるま (a Japanese car), にほんごの せんせい (a teacher of Japanese). Ask "whose?" with だれの, and drop the second noun when it is obvious: わたしのです means "It's mine." の works the same in polite and casual speech. Later you will meet two other jobs for の: "the red one" and turning a verb into a noun (〜のが すき).

title: これ・それ・あれ — "this, that, that over there"
pattern: これ・それ・あれ・どれ／この〜・その〜・あの〜・どの〜
explanation: これ (this), それ (that) and あれ (that over there) stand on their own: これは なんですか. この, その, あの and どの always need a noun right after them: この かさ, その かばん. Distance is about you and your listener: これ is near you, それ is near your listener, and あれ is away from you both; どれ and どの ask "which?". The same words work in polite and casual speech. Places use the matching set ここ / そこ / あそこ, and "this kind of" uses こんな; both come later.

title: 〜じゃないです — "X is not Y"
pattern: 〜じゃないです・〜ではありません
explanation: To say "X is not Y", swap です for じゃないです: がくせいじゃないです means "I'm not a student." You will also see ではありません and じゃありません; they mean the same but sound more formal, so recognise them and use じゃないです in everyday polite talk. A quick "no" to a yes/no question is いいえ、ちがいます ("No, that's not right"), or いいえ plus the じゃないです sentence. This is for nouns: adjectives make their negative in their own way, the past "wasn't" is じゃなかったです, and the casual ない form comes later.

title: 〜も — "too, also"
explanation: も means "too" or "also" and takes the place of は (or が and を): わたしも がくせいです is "I'm a student too." With a negative it means "not … either": わたしも いしゃじゃないです. Two もs give "both A and B": きょうも あしたも やすみです. Particles like に and で stay in front of it (にも, でも), and it works the same in polite and casual speech. Use plain は, not も, when the second thing is different: おっとは いしゃです。わたしは せんせいです.

title: 〜ね・〜よ — "right?" and "you know"
explanation: ね at the end asks your listener to agree, or shares a feeling you both have: おいしいですね is "It's good, isn't it?" よ tells them something you think they don't know yet: たかいですよ is "It's expensive, you know." Together, よね checks something you are fairly sure of ("…, right?"), and そうですね is the usual way to agree. Both work in polite and casual speech, but go easy on よ with your partner: a lot of it can sound pushy, while ね sounds warm.

title: いくらですか — numbers and prices
pattern: いくらですか・〜{円|えん}です
explanation: Japanese counts in blocks: じゅう (10), ひゃく (100), せん (1,000) and まん (10,000), so 12,000 is いちまん にせん, "one ten-thousand, two thousand". Some combinations change sound: さんびゃく (300), ろっぴゃく (600), はっぴゃく (800), さんぜん (3,000), はっせん (8,000), and 10,000 is always いちまん. Add えん for yen, and ask the price with いくらですか, the polite shop question. Counting objects (ひとつ, ふたつ…) uses a different set of numbers, which comes soon.

title: 〜ます・〜ません — polite verbs
explanation: Polite verbs end in ます, and their negative ends in ません: たべます (eat, will eat), たべません (don't eat, won't eat). Japanese has no separate future tense, so the same form covers "I eat" and "I'll eat"; time words like きょう and あした make it clear. Use ます forms with anyone you aren't close to; with your partner you will later switch to the shorter dictionary form (たべる). For now learn these verbs as whole words: the past (ました) comes soon, and verb groups come with the dictionary form.

title: ここ・そこ・あそこ — "here, there, over there"
pattern: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
explanation: ここ (here), そこ (there, near you) and あそこ (over there) are the place words of the こ・そ・あ set, and どこ asks "where?": トイレは どこですか → あそこです. title: いらっしゃいませ — what shop and café staff say
pattern: いらっしゃいませ・{少々|しょうしょう}お{待|ま}ちください・〜でございます
explanation: Shop, café and hotel staff speak to customers in a very polite style called けいご, and much of it is fixed phrases: いらっしゃいませ (welcome), しょうしょう おまちください (one moment, please), かしこまりました (certainly). title: い-adjectives — "it's tasty / it's not tasty"

pattern: {一人|ひとり}・{二人|ふたり}・〜{人|にん}・{何人|なんにん}

title: あります・います — "there is", "I have"
explanation: To say something is somewhere, use place に, then the thing with が (it marks what exists; が has more uses later), then あります for things (and plans or events) or います for people and animals: れいぞうこに ぎゅうにゅうが あります. title: いつも・よく・ときどき — how often
pattern: いつも・よく・ときどき・あまり〜ません・ぜんぜん〜ません
explanation: These words say how often: いつも (always), よく (often), ときどき (sometimes), たまに (once in a while). あまり (not much) and ぜんぜん (not at all, never) only go with a negative verb: おさけは あまり のみません. They usually sit before the verb or near the start of the sentence, and まいにち and まいあさ work the same way. They are used in polite and casual speech; あまり also softens adjectives (あまり たかくない), which comes later with words like とても.

title: な-adjectives — "quiet, pretty, famous"
explanation: な-adjectives take な before a noun (しずかな カフェ, a quiet café) but drop it before です (しずかです). Their negative works like a noun's: しずかじゃないです, never 〜くないです. title: Dictionary form — the plain verb
pattern: {食|た}べる・{飲|の}む・する・{来|く}る
explanation: Every verb has a plain dictionary form, which you use in casual talk with your partner: なに たべる？ (What shall we eat?). To get the ます form, る-verbs drop る (たべる → たべます), う-verbs change their last u sound to i (のむ → のみます), and the two irregular verbs are する → します and くる → きます. Watch the trap: some う-verbs end in る, like かえる (go home), はいる (enter) and きる (cut), so their ます forms are かえります, はいります and きります. Use this plain form only with people you are close to and keep ます for everyone else; full casual speech, with だ and dropped particles, comes a few points later.

title: 〜がすき — likes and dislikes
pattern: 〜が{好|す}きです・〜が{嫌|きら}いです
explanation: すき (like) and きらい (dislike) are な-adjectives, not verbs, so the thing you like takes が, not を: コーヒーが すきです. だいすき means "love" or "really like", and すきな + noun gives "favourite": すきな たべものは なんですか. きらい sounds strong, so people often say あまり すきじゃないです instead.
